fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. David says, “But the righteous will be glad and rejoice before God; they will celebrate with joy.” The wicked will perish as wax melts before the fire, but the righteous are glad to be there before God. Same moment, two very different reactions.
Close, friend, but that's not what David says. He says the righteous “…will be glad and rejoice before God…” Silence isn't in the verse. He says “…they will celebrate with joy.”

I get why you'd pick that one, friend. Verse 1 says His enemies flee His presence, but for the righteous David says they “…will be glad and rejoice before God…” Hiding faces isn't in the verse. Before God, they are glad.

I like the calm of that one, friend, but it's not in the verse. David says, “…the earth shook and the heavens poured down rain before God…” (Psalm 68:8). The word there is shook, not rested. When God marched through the wasteland, the earth shook.

You got it, baker. David says, “You sent abundant rain, O God; You refreshed Your weary inheritance.” The inheritance was weary, and the rain refreshed it. It's like getting a cold glass of water after a long day on your feet.

I see why you'd think that, friend, but testing isn't in the verse. David says, “You sent abundant rain, O God; You refreshed Your weary inheritance.” To something weary, that rain brought refreshing.

Right on, baker! David says, “O God, from Your bounty You provided for the poor.” The bounty is God's, and the poor are who He provides for. Earlier David calls Him “A father of the fatherless and a defender of widows…” (Psalm 68:5), so this fits.
That sounds nice and orderly, friend, but it's not what the women sing. They say, “Kings and their armies flee in haste…” (Psalm 68:12). Fleeing in haste is a big hurry, not a peaceful surrender.
I can see it, friend, kings and armies on the move. But the women sing that they “…flee in haste…” (Psalm 68:12). The song has them fleeing, not marching.

You got it, baker. The song says, “she who waits at home divides the plunder.” The one who stayed home is the one dividing it up. It's like the one who stayed home watching the oven and still gets to hand out the cookies.

Guards at the gate is a fair thought, friend, but the song never mentions them. It says kings and their armies flee in haste, then “she who waits at home divides the plunder.” The song doesn't put anyone at a gate. It puts the dividing in the hands of the one waiting at home.

Hundreds is a fair guess, friend, but David gives a much bigger number. He says, “The chariots of God are tens of thousands…” That's tens of thousands, and then thousands of thousands. And he says the Lord is in His sanctuary as He was at Sinai.

I get why you'd think so, friend, but priests aren't in the verse. David says God “…received gifts from men, even from the rebellious, that the LORD God may dwell there.” The gifts are received by God, and the purpose David gives is His dwelling there.
That's a very kingly guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say armies. David says, “Because of Your temple at Jerusalem kings will bring You gifts.” Gifts are what the verse says the kings bring.
That's it, baker. David says, “Envoys will arrive from Egypt; Cush will stretch out her hands to God.” Envoys arrive from Egypt. And Cush, a land south of Egypt, stretches out her hands to God.
Closed gates would be a different song, friend. David says, “…Cush will stretch out her hands to God.” Gates aren't in the verse. Her hands are stretched out to God.

Armies come up in this psalm, friend, but not in this verse. David says envoys will arrive from Egypt, and “…Cush will stretch out her hands to God.” Stretching out hands is a reaching, not a marching.
Not quite, friend. David says God's “…majesty is over Israel, whose strength is in the skies.” The verse puts His strength in the skies, not down on the earth.

You got it, baker. David says, “Ascribe the power to God, whose majesty is over Israel, whose strength is in the skies.” His majesty is over Israel, and His strength is in the skies. That's where the verse puts it, not down on the ground.
